"Implement the solution in src/lib.rs so that the tests in tests/fizzy.rs pass. The specification follows.

# Description

FizzBuzz is a children's game of counting through the integers. For each of them, if it's divisible by three, substitute the word \"fizz\"; if divisible by five, substitute \"buzz\"; if both, say both; if neither, say the number. It is not particularly difficult to implement, though it enjoyed some popularity for a time as [a quick way to tell whether entry-level programming applicants knew how to program _at all_](https://blog.codinghorror.com/why-cant-programmers-program/).

It has since fallen somewhat into disfavor for that task, because applicants began memorizing FizzBuzz implementations instead of learning to program.

We're going to do something more interesting than the basics: your task in this exercise is to implement FizzBuzz:

- with fully-customizable rules about what numbers produce what words
- fully generic on a very restricted minimal trait set
- such that it works just as well for the Collatz Sequence as for steadily increasing numbers
- with convenient helpers to make its use ergonomic


Do NOT modify the tests or the build files except as stated below. Do not create new files unless the specification requires them; Helper modules may go under src/; you may add [dependencies] from the offline crates listed in OFFLINE_CRATES.md to Cargo.toml."

```rust
use std::fmt::Display;
use std::ops::Rem;

/// A Matcher is a single rule of fizzbuzz: given a function on T, should
/// a word be substituted in? If yes, which word?
pub struct Matcher<T> {
    matcher: Box<dyn Fn(T) -> bool>,
    sub: String,
}

impl<T> Matcher<T> {
    pub fn new<F, S>(matcher: F, subs: S) -> Matcher<T>
    where
        F: Fn(T) -> bool + 'static,
        S: Into<String>,
    {
        Matcher {
            matcher: Box::new(matcher),
            sub: subs.into(),
        }
    }
}

/// A Fizzy is a set of matchers, which may be applied to an iterator.
pub struct Fizzy<T> {
    matchers: Vec<Matcher<T>>,
}

impl<T> Fizzy<T> {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Fizzy {
            matchers: Vec::new(),
        }
    }

    #[must_use]
    pub fn add_matcher(mut self, matcher: Matcher<T>) -> Self {
        self.matchers.push(matcher);
        self
    }

    /// map this fizzy onto every element of an iterator, returning a new iterator
    pub fn apply<I>(self, iter: I) -> impl Iterator<Item = String>
    where
        I: Iterator<Item = T>,
        T: Copy + Display,
    {
        iter.map(move |n| {
            let mut result = String::new();
            for matcher in &self.matchers {
                if (matcher.matcher)(n) {
                    result.push_str(&matcher.sub);
                }
            }
            if result.is_empty() {
                result = n.to_string();
            }
            result
        })
    }
}

/// convenience function: return a Fizzy which applies the standard fizz-buzz rules
pub fn fizz_buzz<T>() -> Fizzy<T>
where
    T: Copy + Rem<Output = T> + PartialEq + From<u8>,
{
    Fizzy::new()
        .add_matcher(Matcher::new(|n: T| n % 3u8.into() == 0u8.into(), "fizz"))
        .add_matcher(Matcher::new(|n: T| n % 5u8.into() == 0u8.into(), "buzz"))
}
```

## What I implemented in `src/lib.rs`

The key design decisions, driven by the tests:

**`Matcher<T>`** — stores a type-erased predicate and a word:
- `matcher: Box<dyn Fn(T) -> bool>` — the rule; `new<F, S>` bounds `F: Fn(T) -> bool + 'static` and `S: Into<String>`, so it accepts closures like `|n: i32| n % 5 == 0` and string literals like `"Buzz"`.

**`Fizzy<T>`** — a `Vec<Matcher<T>>` with a builder-style `add_matcher` and an `apply` method:
- `apply` maps each element through every matcher in insertion order, concatenating matching words; if none match, it falls back to the number via `Display`. Bounds are `T: Copy + Display` — `Copy` is needed because each matcher consumes `T` by value and we call them in a loop.

**`fizz_buzz<T>()`** — builds the standard rules with bounds `T: Rem<Output = T> + PartialEq + From<u8>`. The literals `3`/`5`/`0` are converted with `u8.into()`, which is what makes it work for the custom `Fizzable` type in `minimal_generic_bounds` (which only implements `From<u8>`, `Rem`, `PartialEq`, `Display`, `Add` — no `Ord`, no `num-traits`).

This minimal bound set is exactly what lets it work for `i32`, `u8`, `u64`, `f64`, the Collatz sequence, and the custom `Fizzable` type alike. I made no changes to the tests or build files, and no dependencies were needed.
